headline: Kimi K2.6 outperforms K2.5 with +1.9pp baseline gain, competitive with Sonnet 4.5
summary: An early evaluation of Kimi K2.6 reveals a significant performance boost over K2.5, solving four more skills unaided. Crucially, agent skills continue to provide substantial uplift even as the underlying models become more capable.
details: Moonshot's Kimi K2.6 model demonstrates a +1.9 percentage point baseline gain over its predecessor, K2.5, in a Tessl agent skill evaluation. The new model also resolved two regressions present in K2.5 and now solves four additional skills without requiring any installed assistance.

Initial comparisons place Kimi K2.6 as competitive with Claude Sonnet 4.5 across the same 21 skills and evaluation rubrics. This early signal suggests Kimi 2.6 is comparable to leading providers in the task categories covered by these skills.

A key finding indicates that the uplift provided by agent skills does not diminish as the solver model improves. Both the baseline and with-skill scores move together, maintaining the skill's contribution in a consistent range.

The evaluation also highlighted a nuance in skill transferability: skills prescribing ecosystem-specific tool calls tend to lose more effectiveness in cross-family handoffs. Conversely, skills graded against real, verifiable behaviors, such as actual CLI flags or API shapes, transfer more readily.

These results are based on early signals from one pre-release evaluation on a specific set of 21 skills. A more comprehensive cross-model analysis with clean baselines across all three solvers (Kimi K2.5, Kimi K2.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.5) is currently underway and will be published separately.

headline_marked: [[AI Agent Blind Spot Detector]] helps find failed conversations before they become churn
headline: AI Agent Blind Spot Detector helps find failed conversations before they become churn
summary: Traditional AI agent monitoring often misses critical user failures, even when system metrics look fine, leading to customer churn. This detector focuses on actual conversation outcomes.
details: Production AI agents can appear healthy while silently failing users, with logs showing '200 OK' even as customers abandon conversations. Traditional infrastructure metrics like token cost or latency don't reveal if the agent actually helped the user complete their intent.

An AI agent blind spot detector provides a practical layer to read real conversations and identify unresolved intents. It helps product and engineering teams find and fix repeated failures, offering a useful architecture for builders.

Unlike traditional monitoring that alerts on clear system failures, AI agents can fail silently, returning text without resolving the user's issue. This necessitates a second layer of quality intelligence focused on user intent and agent failure modes.

The detector starts by defining a 'conversation outcome' object. It goes beyond mere negative sentiment to categorize different failure modes, providing actionable insights into where the agent disappoints users.

Key to this is an outcome scorer that checks practical completion signals, such as requested answers, tool success, or user confirmation. It combines deterministic checks with model judgment, avoiding sole reliance on LLM-as-judge.

Clustering failures by 'fix type' rather than just topic is crucial for actionability. This helps teams identify common underlying product or agent issues that require specific engineering solutions, like needing a new tool.

Connecting conversation outcomes to engineering evidence (e.g., prompt version, model, retrieval results, tool calls) enhances usefulness. This allows teams to pinpoint exactly what caused a non-resolution and track fixes.
